subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Solve the equation 8x³ − 36x² − 18x + 81 = 0, the roots being in A.P.

mark_split.label: Take the roots as a − d, a, a + d

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.25 — LAQ chapter 2 Theory of Equations, answer 16. Printed appearances: AP 17 · TS 22. THE MARK SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S: the page prints [1 Mark] against the assumption, [1 Mark] against S₁, [1 Mark] against a = 3/2, [1 Mark] against S₃, [1 Mark] against d = ±3 and [2 Marks] against the roots (1+1+1+1+1+2 = 7), and the card follows it exactly. The SAME step ids (s1_assume, s2_sum, s3_a, s4_product, s5_d, s6_roots) and the same 1+1+1+1+1+2 shape are used on answers 16, 18 and the practice question under 16, deliberately: they are one method — roots a − d, a, a + d, S₁ gives a, S₃ gives d — over different numbers. The book's chapter header carries ★★★; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q19 is the Theory of Equations slot (blueprint, book p.3; all five model papers pp.111–120 agree). Model Paper 3 Q19 (book p.116) is this question; the Bullet Model Paper re-solves it under Q19 on book p.105 — arithmetic cross-checked, identical. Truth check: the roots −3/2, 3/2, 9/2 have equal gaps of 3, add to 9/2 = −a₁/a₀, and their pairwise products add to −9/4 + 27/4 − 27/4 = −9/4 = a₂/a₀, the relation the book never uses. Correction to the book: none. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. recall_prompt: Say how you would solve a cubic whose roots are in A.P. — how you name the roots, which two relations you use, and what each one gives you.
insider_note: Two of the seven marks are the final three numbers; d = −3 is not a second answer, it lists the same roots in the other order.

steps.label: Roots in A.P.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The A.P. form a − d, a, a + d is the whole idea: it makes the sum collapse to 3a. Also write out a₀ … a₃ so the sign rules can be applied without a slip.
lines: The roots are in A.P., so take them as

recall.must_convey: That the three roots are written as a − d, a, a + d because they are in A.P.
accept: take the roots as a minus d, a, a plus d because they are in arithmetic progression
write the three roots as a minus d a and a plus d
roots in A P so let them be a minus d a a plus d
roots A P lo unnayi kabatti a minus d, a, a plus d ga teeskovali
use the symmetric form a minus d a a plus d for the roots
reject: let the roots be alpha beta gamma

steps.why: Writing the roots as a − d, a, a + d builds the A.P. condition into the letters, and it makes the sum collapse to 3a — one relation, one unknown. Letters chosen this way do half the work before any arithmetic starts.
common_mistakes: Using α, β, γ and never bringing in the A.P. condition.
Writing the roots as a, a + d, a + 2d, which works but makes the sum 3a + 3d and the arithmetic longer.

steps.label: Sum of roots
steps.margin_note: Second mark. S₁ = −a₁/a₀ = 36/8 = 9/2. The two d's cancel, so the left side is just 3a.

recall.must_convey: That the sum of the three roots equals −a₁/a₀ = 9/2, and that the d terms cancel in the sum.
accept: sum of the roots is minus a one by a naught which is 9/2
add the three roots, the d's cancel, and the sum is 9/2
S one equals 9/2 from the coefficients
roots sum minus a one by a naught, ante 9/2
the sum of roots comes from the x squared coefficient and is 9/2
heard_as: minus a one by a naught

steps.why: For a₀x³ + a₁x² + a₂x + a₃ = 0 the sum of the roots is −a₁/a₀ — note the minus. With the symmetric letters the ±d cancel, so the sum relation contains a alone.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign in S₁ = −a₁/a₀.
Dividing by the constant term instead of the leading coefficient.
Not cancelling the fraction before writing 3a = …

steps.label: Find a
steps.margin_note: Third mark. 3a = 9/2 gives a = 3/2, the middle root.

recall.must_convey: That 3a equals the sum, so a = 3/2.
accept: three a equals the sum so a is 3/2
the middle root a comes out as 3/2
divide the sum by three to get a equals 3/2
three a ante sum, kabatti a equals 3/2
a is one third of the sum, 3/2

steps.why: Because the sum is 3a exactly, a is found before d is even touched. a is the middle root, so the other two sit at equal distances d on either side of it.
common_mistakes: Writing a = the sum instead of a = the sum divided by 3.

steps.label: Product of roots
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. S₃ = −a₃/a₀ = −81/8 = −81/8. (a − d)(a + d) is a difference of squares, so the product is a(a² − d²).

recall.must_convey: That the product of the three roots equals −a₃/a₀ = −81/8, and that (a − d)·a·(a + d) = a(a² − d²).
accept: product of the roots is minus a three by a naught which is −81/8 and it equals a times a squared minus d squared
multiply the three roots, a minus d times a plus d is a squared minus d squared, and set it equal to −81/8
S three equals −81/8 gives a times a square minus d square
roots product minus a three by a naught, ante −81/8, a into a square minus d square
the product of roots comes from the constant term and equals −81/8

steps.why: The product of the roots is −a₃/a₀ — again a minus, because the constant term is a₃. (a − d)(a + d) = a² − d², so with a known the product relation has only d² in it.
common_mistakes: Writing S₃ = a₃/a₀ and losing the minus.
Expanding (a − d)·a·(a + d) as a³ − d² instead of a(a² − d²).
Using the x coefficient a₂ instead of the constant a₃.

steps.label: Find d
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Put a = 3/2 in, divide out the a, and solve for d². d = ±3; either sign gives the same three roots.

recall.must_convey: That a is substituted into the product relation and solved for d², giving d = ±3.
accept: put a into the product equation and solve for d squared, d is ±3
substitute a and get d squared, so d equals ±3
solve the product relation for d which is ±3
a value petti d square kanukkovali, d equals ±3
d comes from the product relation as ±3

steps.why: d² is what the product relation gives; d = ± its square root. Both signs produce the same three numbers in a different order, so either one may be used.
common_mistakes: A slip when dividing both sides by the fraction a.
Forgetting the ± when taking the square root, and never noticing it does not matter.
Leaving d² = 9 as if d were 9.

steps.label: The three roots
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Substitute a and d back; the three numbers must have equal gaps and must add to the sum found in step 2.
lines: Take d = 3 (d = −3 gives the same three roots):

recall.must_convey: That a and d are put back into a − d, a, a + d to give the roots −3/2, 3/2, 9/2, and that the sign of d does not change the set of roots.
accept: put a and d back into a minus d a a plus d and the roots are −3/2, 3/2, 9/2
the three roots are −3/2, 3/2, 9/2
substitute a and d and list the roots, the other sign of d gives the same three
a, d values petti roots −3/2, 3/2, 9/2 vasthai
write out a minus d a and a plus d with the numbers

steps.why: Substituting back is the check as much as the answer: the three numbers must be in A.P. (equal gaps) and must satisfy the sum found in step 2. A wrong sign anywhere shows up here.
common_mistakes: Listing a and d as the roots.
Not substituting one root back into the equation (each must give 0).
Leaving the fractions unsimplified so the A.P. is not visible.
